subject: Post-call: Redwood vs Hyperscalers — reliability tests & next steps
messages:
From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>
To: Elaine Harris <elaine.harris@edgetech.ai>, Tom Wu <tom.wu@cloudinfra.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-03-08T11:05:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call: Redwood vs Hyperscalers — reliability tests & next steps

Hi Elaine / Tom —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick written recap so we’re aligned and can move to practical tests. High-level takeaways:

- Primary ask: validate behavior under sustained traffic, failover characteristics across regions, and rate-limit/retry behavior compared to the hyperscaler endpoints you’re evaluating.
- What we heard: EdgeTech cares most about predictable tail latency (p95/p99), transparent rate-limit policies (to avoid silent 429s), and deterministic recovery during region-level outages. Procurement/security want SOC2 artifacts and a short list of data-retention assurances.

Where Redwood stands (summary of differentiators):
- Smart routing + graceful fallbacks: automatic routing to standby capacity and model-compatible fallbacks; can be configured for zero-downtime failover or graceful degradation.
- Observable SLO matrix: token-level latency, request tracing, per-route error budget dashboards and automatic alerts (we’ll share the SLO matrix).
- Cost controls and batching knobs: explicit batch sizing and prefix caching to reduce token cost without surprising variance.
- Dedicated capacity option: predictable throughput and isolation vs shared hyperscaler endpoints that may exhibit noisy-neighbor effects under high parallelism.

Suggested next tests (proposed by Redwood):
1) Availability / failover test — simulate region outage and measure recovery window. Goal: failover < 60s with no more than 1% increase in p95.
2) Rate-limit ramp test — ramp to 500 req/s for 30 minutes, then a spike to 800 req/s for 5 minutes. Capture 429 count, retry success, and recovery latency.
3) Error-budget burn emulation — synthetic 5% injected error rate for 15 minutes to observe circuit-breaker and degraded-path behavior.
4) KV/prefix cache reuse test — long-running session that exercises KV cache reuse across requests to measure token-cost delta and p95 improvement.

Metrics to collect: p50/p95/p99 latencies, 429/5xx counts, retries per request, tokens/sec, and recovery time after simulated outage.

What Redwood will provide:
- Test harness (Locust scripts + JMeter profiles) and two endpoints: hosted (shared) and dedicated (provisioned for the run).
- A pre-filled SLO matrix (attached) with expected thresholds and measurement definitions.
- A short runbook for how we’ll simulate region failover (DNS/route withdrawal + standby region redirect).

Your asks we need to cover: SOC2 evidence (we’ll attach SOC2 summary), procurement contact for a short NDA/PO path, and any rate-limit SLAs you want Redwood to validate.

Proposed timeline:
- Run prep + share harness by Tue 2026-03-10
- Execute first baseline tests Wed 2026-03-11
- Deliver initial comparison report Thu 2026-03-12

Please confirm if this scope looks right and whether procurement/security should be looped in before we share the test artifacts.

Attachments: redwood-slo-matrix.xlsx, suggested-load-profile.yaml

Thanks,

Vivek Kulkarni

Thanks Vivek — this is exactly the level of detail we wanted. Couple quick clarifications:

- Can you include procurement in the thread? Our procurement lead is Sara Mills (sara.mills@edgetech.ai) — she’ll own PO/timeline.
- Security: we will need the SOC2 Type II report and a short note on data retention and encryption at rest/transport before we run anything in a shared environment.
- For the rate-limit test, can you also record client-side retry behavior (client backoff + jitter) so we can compare hyperscaler adoption patterns vs Redwood’s retry guidance?

Also looping Tom to ensure the workload shapes reflect our internal traffic patterns (Tom — we run a lot of short-lived chat sessions with average context ~650 tokens; peak concurrency tends to be around 450–550 simultaneous sessions in US-WEST).

If possible we’d like the first baseline to run later this week — Thu or Fri.

Subject: Re: Post-call: Redwood vs Hyperscalers — reliability tests & next steps

Hi all — internal technical follow-up with the concrete plan for tests. Re-stating with more engineering detail so procurement/security can see we’re not starting blind.

Test harness & infra:
- Scripts: Locust + a single-node runner to coordinate CSV session seeds (we’ll provide the seed set to emulate your 650-token chats). See Drive: https://drive.redwood.ai/shared/load-tests/edgetech-hyperscaler-comparison.zip (contains locustfile.py, runbook, and sample traffic seeds).
- Endpoints:
  * Hosted (shared): https://api.redwood.ai/v1/edgetech-test-hosted (rate-limited per account)
  * Dedicated: temporary dedicated pool provisioned in us-west-2 for the run (explicitly isolated)

Phases:
- Phase 1 (baseline): 100 rps steady-state for 20 minutes — capture p95/p99 and 429/5xx baseline.
- Phase 2 (ramp): linear ramp to 500 rps over 10 minutes, sustain 500 rps for 30 minutes. Spike to 800 rps for 5 minutes.
- Phase 3 (failover): simulate region outage by withdrawing route from us-west-2 for 90 seconds and failover to us-east-1. Measure recovery time and request failures during transition.
- Phase 4 (cache test): maintain 300 concurrent sessions for 30 minutes with repeated prompt prefixes to measure KV/prefix cache hit rate and token-cost reductions.

Measurement & targets (we’ll log with distributed tracing tags):
- Target p95 < 200ms on dedicated under 500 rps for 650-token average workloads.
- Target recovery window < 60s for automated failover when using our recommended routing policy.
- Record all 429s + server-side retry success rates and backoff timings.

Security/artifacts:
- SOC2 Type II summary & encrypt-at-rest note attached to this email thread (I’ve uploaded a redacted copy to the Drive link).

Attachments: redwood-slo-matrix.xlsx (same as shared), suggested-load-profile.yaml

Open questions for EdgeTech:
- Is the dedicated run acceptable for procurement? If yes, we’ll provision the pool for the test window.
- Any preferred maintenance blackout windows? We want to avoid your production change windows.

If you confirm the plan I’ll schedule the Locust runner and provision the dedicated pool.

—Marissa
